To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effects of Cu on soil microbes are different from those of Ni and Zn and that microbial responses to metal inputs are not additive.
the microbial response to metal inputs in soil was complex and depended on the metal(s) applied and the time since application.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of sewage sludge on the microbial activity in grassland soils.
the effects of metals on the soil microbial community and the potential use of microbial parameters to predict metal toxicity.
the effect of heavy metal inputs from sewage sludge on soil microbial activity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
metal inputs at rates close to current limits affect microbial processes in grassland soil.
microbial responses to metal inputs were complex, and varied with the metal and the combination of metals.
microbial activity is affected by metal inputs in sewage sludge, and that the response is dependent upon the metal, its level, its combination with others and time of sampling after application.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
microbial activity is affected by Cu, Ni and to some extent Zn inputs, with the response being dependent on the time after sludge addition, the metal applied and the metal combination.
Cu and Zn have similar effects on microbial processes in soils, but that Ni can be more toxic than Cu.
microbial responses to metals are dependent upon metal type and concentration and the time after metal application.
The main takeaway from our work is that
microbial responses to metals in soil can be complex.
the microbial community in soil is sensitive to metals in the environment.
Cu has a greater potential to impact on soil microbial processes than either Ni or Zn.
